story.heading: Everything in one place, before you need it
paragraphs: When something goes wrong, such as a power cut, a storm, a sudden hospital visit or a quick evacuation, the information you need is often scattered across phones, drawers and memories. This binder gathers it into one place, so you, or anyone helping you, can find it in seconds.
Fill it in on screen and save it, or print the blank pages and write by hand. Every field is a clear box or line, margins are safe for home printers, and the pages read well in black and white.

It is written for households in any country. You add your own local emergency number, water amounts appear in both liters and US gallons, and there is a cross-border section for families with papers, property or relatives in more than one country.

story.heading: A tracker that keeps it current
paragraphs: A binder is only useful if it is up to date. The companion spreadsheet lists your stored supplies and your documents (passports, ID cards, residence permits, insurance policies, vehicle papers) with their expiry dates. Each row shows the days left and a clear status: OK, Expires soon, Expired or No date.
A dashboard counts what needs attention, a calculator works out water and food targets for your household, and a review tab tells you when your next six-month check is due.
story.note_html: Private by design. The binder records where things are and who to call. It never asks for passwords, PINs, full account or card numbers, document numbers or crypto seed phrases.

story.heading: Decide once a week, not every evening
paragraphs: The question "what's for dinner?" is easier to answer on a quiet Sunday than at six o'clock on a busy Tuesday. This planner turns it into a short weekly routine: check what you already have, choose the week's meals, write one grocery list, and shop once.

Start by filling in a few setup pages: who you cook for and what they love or avoid, which nights are busy, a handful of theme nights, and a bank of go-to meals your household already enjoys. After that, planning a week is mostly picking from your own list.

Every weekly plan has space for breakfast, lunch, dinner and snacks, a busy-night tick for each day, and boxes for what to prep ahead, what to use up first and how to handle leftovers. The facing grocery list is grouped by store section, so you walk each aisle once.

story.heading: A spreadsheet that writes the grocery list
paragraphs: The companion spreadsheet works in Microsoft Excel and Google Sheets. List your meals and their ingredients once, mark what you usually keep in stock, then choose the week's meals from drop-down lists. Every ingredient you need and don't have appears on the Grocery List tab, with its store section and the meal it is for.
There is also a pantry stock count that flags items to restock, and a simple spend log with weekly and monthly totals in any currency.
story.note_html: Made for any kitchen. Units are flexible, a conversions page covers cups, grams, ounces and oven temperatures in Celsius, Fahrenheit and gas marks, and nothing assumes a particular country, store or diet.
